clue.text: Noteworthy gesture

blocks.note: first meaning: an adjective for something striking or remarkable
second meaning: a noun for a movement made to convey a message

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a gesture worth noticing; the two words are separate meanings, one adjective and one noun.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective the word means remarkable (a signal victory); as a noun it is a sign or motion conveying information.

clue.text: One may help you along the way

definitions.text: One may help you along the way

blocks.clueFragment: One may help you along the way
blocks.note: surface reading: a kind friend or mentor who assists you through life
setter's reading: 'the way' is literally a road, and the helper is a roadside pointer showing directions

explanation.walkthrough: 'Along the way' is an idiom for 'during life', but read literally it is a road, where a pointer at a junction helps travellers.
explanation.definitionFit: A post at a roadside bearing arms that point travellers toward places literally helps them along their route.

clue.text: Drink teenager brewed

indicators.note: brewing mixes and transforms ingredients, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A young person makes themselves a cup of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Green tea is an unfermented tea, a hot beverage, so it is an example of a drink.

clue.text: A passage from Australia is lengthy

indicators.note: 'from' says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows, unchanged

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word, the whole second word, and the first two letters of the third

explanation.surface: A long excerpt taken from a book about Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: An aisle is a walkway between rows of seats or shelves, which is a passage.

clue.text: They may provide openings for a rock band

blocks.note: first meaning: the hinged panels through which you enter rooms
second meaning: the American group fronted by Jim Morrison

explanation.surface: Some people offer a music group its big breaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Openings' seems to mean opportunities or support slots for a group; it is also simply what doors make.
explanation.definitionFit: Doors open entryways, and The Doors were a 1960s Los Angeles rock group led by singer Jim Morrison.

clue.text: Choice phrase?

blocks.note: surface reading: a choice phrase is a well-chosen, excellent expression
setter's reading: a phrase used when offering someone a choice, as when a coin is tossed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Choice' as an adjective means select or fine; here it is a noun, and the phrase is the call made when a coin is flipped to decide something.
explanation.definitionFit: Before tossing a coin, one person asks the other to call one of two sides, so this is literally the phrase offering a choice.

clue.text: See sister in party dress about noon

blocks.note: a do is an informal word for a party
a mini is a short dress or skirt
ca is the abbreviation of circa, about
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: Look at the nun who has come to the party in a dress, around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' merely invites the solver to look at the nun; 'in' joins her to the wordplay, which reads as one picture of a nun dressed for a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dominican is a member of the Catholic order founded by St Dominic, and its nuns are called sisters.

clue.text: Decorated knight brought in to give a speech

indicators.note: something brought in is placed inside, so the first piece sits within the second

blocks.note: N is the chess notation for a knight
to orate is to deliver a formal speech

explanation.surface: A decorated knight is invited in to deliver an address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decorated knight' reads as one honoured person, but 'Decorated' is the definition and the knight is just a chess letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornate means elaborately adorned, so something decorated heavily can be described this way.

clue.text: Drink readily available after opening of saloon

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that letter is taken
'after' places the first piece named behind the one that follows it

blocks.note: the first letter of saloon
handy means close at hand, ready to use

explanation.surface: A drink is easy to come by once the saloon bar opens.
explanation.walkthrough: A shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, a common British pub drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Shandy is a drink of beer diluted with lemonade or ginger beer.

clue.text: Greek leisure film

blocks.note: GR is an abbreviation for Greek
ease is freedom from work, relaxed leisure

explanation.surface: A movie about relaxation in Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: Grease is the 1978 musical film starring John Travolta and Olivia Newton-John.

clue.text: Samaritan surprisingly run off island

indicators.note: something done surprisingly comes out unexpectedly, so the letters land in an unexpected order
'off' tells us the named letter is taken away from the word

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

explanation.surface: A good Samaritan unexpectedly runs away from an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the R from the word Samaritan, then rearrange the remaining eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasmania is the large island state lying south of the Australian mainland.

clue.text: Uncompromising in nets training bats

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters have gone mad and are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A stubborn cricketer practising in the nets with the bats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bats' looks like cricket equipment, but it is the slang adjective meaning crazy; nets are the netted practice lanes where cricketers train.
explanation.definitionFit: Intransigent describes someone who refuses to change their views or yield, which is being unwilling to compromise.

clue.text: Novel writer - Wheatley, say

blocks.note: a pen is the instrument a person writes with
Dennis Wheatley was a British thriller writer, so Wheatley is an example of someone called Dennis

explanation.surface: A novelist such as Wheatley.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites a writer's name, but 'writer' is the thing you write with and Wheatley yields his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pendennis is an 1848–50 novel by William Makepeace Thackeray, so it is an example of a novel.

clue.text: Well-known college rejected daughter

indicators.note: something rejected is turned back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: Eton is the famous English public school, Eton College
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A famous college turned away someone's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means famous or renowned, a direct synonym of being widely known.

clue.text: Perry's accent confused actor

indicators.note: confused letters are muddled up, so they must be put into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone called Perry has a muddled, hard-to-place accent that puzzles a performer.
explanation.definitionFit: Spencer Tracy was a two-time Oscar-winning Hollywood film star, so he is an example of an actor.

clue.text: Not quite covered, rounding tree, bullets coming from all sides

indicators.note: not quite complete means the word stops one letter short of its end
rounding means going around something, so one piece is wrapped about another

blocks.note: to cover a distance is to cross it
a fir is a coniferous tree

explanation.surface: Someone only partly in cover, running round a tree as shots come from every direction.
explanation.walkthrough: To cover a distance is to cross it; the past tense loses its final letter and wraps round the conifer.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossfire is gunfire from two or more directions whose lines intersect, catching anyone caught between them.

clue.text: Greek character, in ancient Greek city, almost singled out

indicators.note: 'in' places the first piece inside the second
almost means not entirely, so the last letter of the word is left off

blocks.note: eta is the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet
Sparta was the militaristic city-state of ancient Greece

explanation.surface: A Greek figure, picked out from the crowd in an old Greek city.
explanation.walkthrough: Both Greek references are real here: the letter and the city-state, cut short by one letter, supply all the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To set apart is to distinguish someone or keep them separate, which is what singling out does.

clue.text: A depression engulfing that female supporter

indicators.note: to engulf is to swallow up, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: taken as written
her is the pronoun for that woman
a dent is a small hollow or depression in a surface

explanation.surface: A slump in mood swallows up a woman who backs a cause.
explanation.definitionFit: An adherent is a follower or backer of a party, leader or belief, so a supporter.

clue.text: Jet he'd taken round area in spring

indicators.note: taken round means carried about something, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: a fountain is a jet of water shooting upward
taken as written, without the apostrophe
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A man has been carried around some region in a jet aircraft during springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jet' and 'spring' look like an aircraft and a season; they are a spurt of water and a source of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A fountainhead is the source of a stream, and a spring is likewise where water rises from the ground.

clue.text: A launch at sea

blocks.note: taken as written
to float a company or idea is to launch it

explanation.surface: A boat is launched out on the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Launch' suggests a motorboat, but it is the verb meaning to put a company onto the market.
explanation.definitionFit: Something afloat is floating on water, so it is at sea rather than on land.

clue.text: Fellow, say, visiting a wine shop

blocks.note: bod is British slang for a person or fellow
e.g., for example, is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man, for instance, calls in at a wine shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodega is a Spanish wine cellar or wine shop; in the US the word also means a corner store.

clue.text: Female victim in Eliot's river

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for female
a loss is a casualty, someone killed or hurt in battle

explanation.surface: A woman drowned in a river in a George Eliot novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls Maggie Tulliver, who drowns at the end of George Eliot's novel The Mill on the Floss.
explanation.definitionFit: The Floss is the river on which the mill stands in The Mill on the Floss, George Eliot's novel.

clue.text: Unlucky, a guy unable to relax

blocks.note: ill means unfortunate, as in ill luck
taken as written
to guy someone is to mock or make fun of them

explanation.surface: An unfortunate man cannot unwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a noun for a man, but it is a verb meaning to ridicule.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ill at ease means uncomfortable or nervous, so a person in that state cannot settle or relax.

clue.text: Under emotional strain in past, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: nervous and anxious
second meaning: a grammatical form of a verb, of which the past is one example

explanation.surface: Someone was stressed at some time gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks the past as just one example of the grammatical category.
explanation.definitionFit: Tense is both an adjective for nervy strain and a grammar noun for verb forms like past, present and future.

clue.text: Quick joke about English ship

blocks.note: on means concerning, as in a book on birds
E is the abbreviation for English
a liner is a large passenger ship

explanation.surface: A brief gag about a vessel from England.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-liner is a short joke or witty remark delivered in a single sentence.

clue.text: I name patient as a precaution

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name
doctors refer to a patient under treatment as a case

explanation.surface: A doctor identifies a patient, just to be safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patient' looks like an adjective meaning tolerant; it is the noun for someone receiving care.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something just in case means doing it to guard against a possible event, which is acting as a precaution.

clue.text: Attempt to fix a match, all but a farce

indicators.note: all but means everything except one letter, so the word loses its last
to fix something in place is to set it inside a holder, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a try is an attempt
a vesta is a short match, especially a wax one

explanation.surface: An effort to rig a sporting fixture was little short of a farce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix a match' suggests match-fixing in sport, but the match is one that is struck to make fire, named after Vesta, the Roman goddess of the hearth.
explanation.definitionFit: A travesty is an absurd or grotesque imitation of something, which is a farce in the figurative sense.

clue.text: Go away, exhausted, with Italian

blocks.note: beat is informal for worn out
It is the abbreviation for Italian

explanation.surface: An exhausted Italian is told to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Beat it is a slang command telling someone to leave at once, an idiom for clear off.
